danish.title: Tredje bog (1805) — Kapitel 6
paragraphs: Det var længe siden, Rostov-familien havde haft nyheder fra Nikolaj (Nikolenka). Først midt på vinteren blev greven endelig overrakt et brev, skrevet med sønnens håndskrift. Da han modtog det, løb han på tåspidserne til sit arbejdsværelse i ængstelse og hast, mens han forsøgte at undgå opmærksomhed, lukkede døren og begyndte at læse brevet.
Anna Mikhajlovna, der altid vidste alt, hvad der foregik i huset, var ved at høre om brevets ankomst stille gået ind i stuen og fandt greven med det i hånden, hulkende og leende på samme tid.
Anna Mikhajlovna boede stadig hos Rostov-familien, skønt hendes kår var forbedrede.
»Min kære ven?« sagde hun i en medfølende, spørgende tone, parat til at vise deltagelse på enhver måde.
Greven hulkede endnu mere.
»Nikolenka... et brev... sår... såret... min kære dreng... grevinden... forfremmet til officer... Gudskelov... Hvordan fortæller man den lille grevinde!«

Anna Mikhajlovna satte sig ved hans side, tørrede med sit eget lommetørklæde tårerne fra hans øjne og fra brevet, tørrede derefter sine egne øjne, trøstede greven og besluttede, at hun ved middagen og indtil tetid ville forberede grevinden, og at hun efter teen med Guds hjælp ville fortælle hende det.

Til middag talte Anna Mikhajlovna hele tiden om krigsnyheder og om Nikolenka, spurgte to gange, hvornår det sidste brev fra ham var modtaget — skønt hun allerede vidste det — og bemærkede, at de meget vel kunne få brev fra ham den dag. Hver gang disse antydninger begyndte at gøre grevinden ængstelig, og hun uroligt kiggede skiftevis på greven og Anna Mikhajlovna, drejede sidstnævnte meget behændigt samtalen hen på ligegyldige emner. Natasja, der af hele familien var den mest begavede til at opfange enhver nuance i tonefald, blik og ansigtsudtryk, spidsede ører fra måltidets begyndelse og var sikker på, at der var en hemmelighed mellem hendes far og Anna Mikhajlovna, at den havde noget med hendes bror at gøre, og at Anna Mikhajlovna forberedte dem. Dristig som hun var, vovede Natasja, der vidste, hvor følsom hendes mor var i alt, der vedrørte Nikolenka, ikke at stille spørgsmål under middagen, men hun var for ophidset til at spise og vred og vendte sig uophørligt på stolen, uanset guvernantens irettesættelser. Efter middagen styrtede hun hovedkulds efter Anna Mikhajlovna, kastede sig om halsen på hende og klamrede sig fast, da hun indhentede hende i opholdsstuen.
»Tante, kære, sig mig hvad det er!«
»Intet, min kære.«
»Nej, kæreste, søde, sødeste, jeg giver mig ikke — jeg ved, at De ved noget.«
Anna Mikhajlovna rystede på hovedet.
»Du er en lille snedighed,« sagde hun.
»Et brev fra Nikolenka! Det er jeg sikker på!« udbrød Natasja, idet hun læste bekræftelsen i Anna Mikhajlovnas ansigt.
»Men for Guds skyld, vær forsigtig — du ved, hvordan det kan påvirke din mamma.«
»Det skal jeg nok, det skal jeg nok, bare fortæl! De vil ikke? Så fortæller jeg det med det samme.«
Anna Mikhajlovna fortalte hende med få ord brevets indhold på betingelse af, at hun ikke fortalte nogen.
»Nej, ved min sande æresord,« sagde Natasja og korsede sig, »jeg fortæller det ikke til nogen!« og hun løb straks hen til Sonja.
»Nikolenka... såret... et brev,« meddelte hun i triumferende glæde.
»Nikolaj!« var alt, Sonja sagde og blev øjeblikkeligt hvid.
Natasja, der så det indtryk, nyheden om broderens sår gjorde på Sonja, følte for første gang den sørgelige side af nyheden.
Hun styrtede hen til Sonja, omfavnede hende og begyndte at græde.
»Et lille sår, men han er blevet officer; han har det godt nu — han skrev selv,« sagde hun gennem tårerne.

»Se! Det er sandt, at alle I kvinder er tudefjæs,« bemærkede Petja, der gik op og ned i stuen med store, beslutsomme skridt. »Nu er jeg meget glad, virkelig glad, for at min bror har udmærket sig så. I er allesammen tårepersere og forstår ingenting.«
Natasja smilede gennem tårerne.
»Du har ikke læst brevet?« spurgte Sonja.
»Nej, men hun sagde, at alt var overstået, og at han nu er officer.«
»Gudskelov!« sagde Sonja og korsede sig. »Men måske sagde hun ikke sandheden. Lad os gå ind til mamma.«
Petja gik en stund tavst op og ned i værelset.

»Hvis jeg havde været i Nikolenkas sted, ville jeg have dræbt endnu flere af de franskmænd,« sagde han. »Sikke nogle væmmelige udyr! Jeg ville have slået så mange ihjel, at der lå en hel bunke af dem.«
»Hold mund, Petja — sikke en gås, du er!«
»Jeg er ikke en gås, men det er I, der tuder over bagateller,« sagde Petja.
»Husker du ham?« spurgte Natasja pludselig efter et øjebliks stilhed.
Sonja smilede.
»Om jeg husker Nikolaj?«

»Nej, Sonja, men husker du ham sådan, at du virkelig husker ham fuldstændigt, husker alt?« sagde Natasja med en udtryksfuld gestus, åbenbart i ønsket om at give sine ord en helt bestemt mening. »Jeg husker også Nikolenka, jeg husker ham godt,« sagde hun. »Men jeg husker ikke Boris. Ham husker jeg overhovedet ikke.«
»Hvad! Du husker ikke Boris?« spurgte Sonja overrasket.

»Det er ikke, at jeg ikke husker — jeg ved, hvordan han ser ud, men ikke som jeg husker Nikolenka. Ham — jeg lukker bare mine øjne og husker, men Boris... Nej!« (Hun lukkede øjnene.) »Nej! Ingenting overhovedet.«

»Åh, Natasja!« sagde Sonja og kiggede henrevet og alvorligt på veninden, som om hun ikke anså hende for værdig til at høre, hvad hun ville sige, og som om hun sagde det til en anden, med hvem man ikke spøger. »Jeg er forelsket i din bror én gang for alle, og hvad end der sker med ham eller med mig, vil jeg aldrig ophøre med at elske ham, så længe jeg lever.«

Natasja kiggede på Sonja med undrende og nysgerrige øjne og sagde intet. Hun følte, at Sonja talte sandt, at der fandtes en sådan kærlighed som den, Sonja talte om. Men Natasja havde endnu ikke selv følt noget lignende. Hun troede, det kunne ske, men forstod det ikke.
»Vil du skrive til ham?« spurgte hun.

Sonja blev eftertænksom. Spørgsmålet om, hvordan hun skulle skrive til Nikolaj, og om hun burde skrive, plagede hende. Nu, da han allerede var officer og såret helt, ville det så være rigtigt at minde ham om sig selv og, som det kunne se ud, om de forpligtelser, han havde påtaget sig over for hende?
»Det ved jeg ikke. Jeg tror, at hvis han skriver, så skriver jeg også,« sagde hun rødmende.
»Og du ville ikke skamme dig over at skrive til ham?«
Sonja smilede.
»Nej.«
»Og jeg ville skamme mig over at skrive til Boris. Det gør jeg ikke.«
»Hvorfor dog det?«
»Åh, det ved jeg ikke. Det er pinligt og ville gøre mig flov.«

»Og jeg ved godt, hvorfor hun ville skamme sig,« sagde Petja, fornærmet over Natasjas tidligere bemærkning. »Det er, fordi hun var forelsket i den tykke med brillerne« (sådan beskrev Petja sin navnebror, den nye grev Bezukhov), »og nu er hun forelsket i den dér sanger« (han mente Natasjas italienske sangmester), »det er derfor, hun skammer sig!«
»Petja, du er dum!« sagde Natasja.
»Ikke dummere end dig, frue,« sagde den niårige Petja med minen af en gammel brigadér.

Grevinden var blevet forberedt af Anna Mikhajlovnas antydninger under middagen. Da hun trak sig tilbage, sad hun i en lænestol med blikket fæstnet på et miniatureportræt af sin søn på låget af en snustobaksdåse, mens tårerne stadig trillede. Anna Mikhajlovna, med brevet, kom på tåspidserne til grevindens dør og standsede.
»Kom ikke ind,« sagde hun til den gamle greve, der fulgte hende. »Kom senere.« Og hun gik ind og lukkede døren bag sig.
Greven satte øret til nøglehullet og lyttede.

Først hørte han lyden af ligegyldige stemmer, derefter Anna Mikhajlovnas stemme alene i en lang tale, så et udråb, så stilhed, og derpå begge stemmer i kor med glade intonationer, og endelig skridt. Anna Mikhajlovna åbnede døren. Hendes ansigt bar det stolte udtryk af en kirurg, der netop har udført en vanskelig operation og lader publikum slippe ind for at beundre hans dygtighed.
»Det er gjort!« sagde hun til greven og pegede triumferende på grevinden, der sad med snustobaksdåsen med portrættet i den ene hånd og brevet i den anden og skiftevis trykkede dem til sine læber.

Da hun fik øje på greven, strakte hun armene ud mod ham, omfavnede hans skaldede hoved, og hen over det kiggede hun atter på brevet og portrættet, og for at trykke dem til sine læber igen skubbede hun let det skaldede hoved til side. Vera, Natasja, Sonja og Petja trådte nu ind, og oplæsningen af brevet begyndte. Efter en kort beskrivelse af felttoget og de to slag, han havde deltaget i, og sin forfremmelse sagde Nikolaj, at han kyssede sin fars og mors hænder og bad om deres velsignelse, og at han kyssede Vera, Natasja og Petja. Desuden sendte han hilsener til monsieur Schelling, madame Schoss og sin gamle barnepige og bad dem kysse for ham »kære Sonja, som han elskede og tænkte på som altid.« Da hun hørte dette, rødmede Sonja, så tårerne kom i øjnene, og ude af stand til at udholde de blikke, der rettedes mod hende, løb hun ind i dansesalen, hvirvlede rundt i den med kjolen oppustet som en ballon og satte sig rødmende og smilende tungt på gulvet. Grevinden græd.
»Hvorfor græder du, mamma?« spurgte Vera. »Ud fra alt, hvad han skriver, burde man jo glæde sig og ikke græde.«
Det var ganske sandt, men greven, grevinden og Natasja kiggede bebrejdende på hende. »Og hvem mon hun kommer efter?« tænkte grevinden.

Nikolajs brev blev læst op hundredvis af gange, og dem, der blev anset for værdige til at høre det, måtte komme til grevinden, for hun slap det ikke af hænderne. Huslærerne kom, og ammerne, og Dmitrij, og adskillige bekendte, og grevinden læste brevet op hver gang med fornyet glæde og fandt hver gang nye beviser på Nikolenkas fortræffeligheder. Hvor mærkeligt, hvor usædvanligt, hvor glædeligt det syntes, at hendes søn — ham, hvis bittesmå lemmers bevægelser hun havde mærket for tyve år siden i sit skød — at den søn, om hvem hun plejede at skændes med den alt for overbærende greve, den søn, der først havde lært at sige »pære« og derefter »bedstemor« — at denne søn nu var langt borte i et fremmed land, midt i fremmede omgivelser, en mandig kriger, der udførte sit eget mandsarbejde uden hjælp eller vejledning. Den almene erfaring fra alle tider, der viser, at børn umærkeligt vokser fra vuggen til voksenlivet, eksisterede ikke for grevinden. Sønnens vækst mod manddommen havde på hvert trin forekommet hende lige så usædvanlig, som om der aldrig havde eksisteret de millioner af mennesker, der voksede op på samme måde. Ligesom det for tyve år siden syntes umuligt, at det lille væsen, der levede et sted under hendes hjerte, nogensinde ville skrige, die hendes bryst og begynde at tale, kunne hun nu ikke tro, at det lille væsen kunne være denne stærke, tapre mand, denne mønsterlige søn og officer, som han ifølge brevet nu var.

»Sikken en stil! Hvor charmerende han beskriver!« sagde hun og læste brevets beskrivende del. »Og sikken en sjæl! Ikke et ord om sig selv... Ikke et ord! Om en Denisov eller nogen, selvom han selv nok er taprere end nogen af dem. Han fortæller intet om sine lidelser. Sikket et hjerte! Hvor det ligner ham! Og han har husket alle! Ikke glemt nogen. Jeg har altid sagt det, da han kun var så høj — jeg har altid sagt det...«

I mere end en uge blev der gjort forberedelser, udkast til breve til Nikolaj fra hele husstanden blev skrevet og renskrevet, og under grevindens opsyn og grevens omsorg blev penge og alt det nødvendige til den nyudnævnte officers uniform og udstyr samlet. Anna Mikhajlovna, den praktiske kvinde, havde endda ved yndest hos militære myndigheder sikret sig fordelagtige kommunikationsveje for sig selv og sin søn. Hun havde lejlighed til at sende sine breve til storfyrst Konstantin Pavlovitj, der kommanderede Garden. Rostov-familien antog, at »Den russiske garde, i felten« var en ganske bestemt adresse, og at hvis et brev nåede storfyrsten, der førte kommandoen over Garden, var der ingen grund til, at det ikke skulle nå frem til Pavlograd-regimentet, der formodentlig lå et sted i nærheden. Og så blev det besluttet at sende brevene og pengene med storfyrstens kurer til Boris, og Boris skulle videresende dem til Nikolaj. Brevene var fra den gamle greve, grevinden, Petja, Vera, Natasja og Sonja, og endelig var der seks tusind rubler til hans udstyr og diverse andet, som den gamle greve sendte sin søn.

english.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: It had been a long time since the Rostovs had any news from Nicholas. It wasn't until the middle of winter that the count was finally handed a letter in his son's handwriting. He grabbed it and hurried to his study on tiptoe, anxious and excited, trying not to be noticed. He shut the door and began to read.

Anna Mikhaylovna, who always knew everything that went on in the house, heard about the letter's arrival and quietly slipped into the room. She found the count holding the letter, sobbing and laughing at the same time.
Anna Mikhaylovna's circumstances had improved, but she was still living with the Rostovs.
"My dear friend?" she said in a tone of sympathetic concern, ready to respond to whatever emotion was called for.
The count sobbed even harder.
"Nikolenka... a letter... he w-was... wounded... my dear boy... the countess... promoted to officer... thank God... How do I tell the countess!"

Anna Mikhaylovna sat down beside him, wiped the tears from his eyes and from the letter with her own handkerchief, then dried her own eyes, comforted the count, and came up with a plan: at dinner and through teatime she would prepare the countess, and after tea, with God's help, she would break the news.

At dinner, Anna Mikhaylovna talked constantly about war news and about Nikolenka, twice asking when the last letter from him had arrived — though she already knew. She kept hinting that they might very well receive a letter from him that day. Each time these hints made the countess anxious — she would glance uneasily at the count and at Anna Mikhaylovna — Anna Mikhaylovna deftly steered the conversation to some trivial topic. Natasha, who had the sharpest instincts of anyone in the family for detecting shifts in tone, expression, and mood, had been alert since the start of the meal. She was certain there was some secret between her father and Anna Mikhaylovna, that it had something to do with her brother, and that Anna Mikhaylovna was laying the groundwork. Bold as she was, Natasha knew how sensitive her mother was about anything involving Nikolenka and didn't dare ask questions at the table. But she was too excited to eat and kept squirming in her chair, ignoring her governess's reprimands. After dinner she rushed after Anna Mikhaylovna and, catching up in the sitting room, threw herself on her neck.
"Auntie, darling, please tell me what it is!"
"It's nothing, my dear."
"No, dearest, sweetest, honey — I won't give up. I know you know something."
Anna Mikhaylovna shook her head.
"You little sneak," she said.
"A letter from Nikolenka! I'm sure of it!" Natasha exclaimed, reading the confirmation in Anna Mikhaylovna's face.
"But for God's sake, be careful — you know how it could affect your mother."
"I will, I will, just tell me! You won't? Then I'll go tell everyone right now."
Anna Mikhaylovna gave her a brief summary of the letter's contents, on the condition that she tell no one.
"No, I swear on my honor," said Natasha, crossing herself, "I won't tell anyone!" And she immediately ran off to find Sonya.
"Nikolenka... wounded... a letter," she announced in gleeful triumph.
"Nicholas!" was all Sonya managed, instantly turning white.
Seeing the impact the news of her brother's wound had on Sonya, Natasha felt for the first time the painful side of it.
She threw her arms around Sonya and began to cry.
"It's just a small wound, but he's been made an officer. He's fine now — he wrote the letter himself," she said through her tears.

"There, you see! All you women are such crybabies," said Petya, striding around the room with large, determined steps. "I'm very glad, very glad indeed, that my brother has distinguished himself. You're all blubberers who don't understand anything."
Natasha smiled through her tears.
"Have you read the letter?" Sonya asked.
"No, but she said it's all over and that he's an officer now."
"Thank God!" said Sonya, crossing herself. "But maybe she wasn't telling the truth. Let's go to Mama."
Petya paced the room in silence for a moment.
"If I'd been in Nikolenka's place, I would have killed even more of those Frenchmen," he said. "What awful brutes they are! I would have killed so many there'd have been a pile of them."
"Be quiet, Petya — you're being ridiculous!"
"I'm not ridiculous — it's the people who cry over nothing who are ridiculous," Petya retorted.
"Do you remember him?" Natasha asked suddenly, after a moment of silence.
Sonya smiled.
"Do I remember Nicholas?"

"No, Sonya, what I mean is — do you remember him so well that you can picture him perfectly, everything about him?" Natasha said with an emphatic gesture, clearly trying to give her words a very specific meaning. "I remember Nikolenka too — I remember him well. But I don't remember Boris. Not at all."
"What! You don't remember Boris?" Sonya asked in surprise.

"It's not that I don't remember — I know what he looks like, but not the way I remember Nikolenka. With him, I just close my eyes and he's there. But Boris..." She shut her eyes. "No! Nothing at all."

"Oh, Natasha!" said Sonya, gazing at her friend with an intensity and seriousness that suggested she was saying something too important for jokes, almost as if speaking to someone else entirely. "I am in love with your brother, once and for all, and whatever may happen to him or to me, I will never stop loving him as long as I live."

Natasha looked at Sonya with curious, wondering eyes and said nothing. She felt that Sonya was telling the truth, that such love existed. But Natasha had never felt anything like it herself. She believed it was possible, but she didn't understand it.
"Will you write to him?" she asked.

Sonya grew thoughtful. The question of how to write to Nicholas, and whether she even should, tormented her. Now that he was an officer and a wounded hero, would it be right to remind him of her existence and of the promises he'd made?
"I don't know. I think if he writes to me, I'll write back," she said, blushing.
"And you wouldn't feel embarrassed writing to him?"
Sonya smiled.
"No."
"Well, I'd be embarrassed to write to Boris. I'm not going to."
"Why would you be embarrassed?"
"I don't know. It's just awkward. It would make me feel strange."

"I know why she'd be embarrassed," said Petya, still stinging from Natasha's earlier remark. "It's because she was in love with that fat one in glasses" — that was how Petya described his namesake, the new Count Bezukhov — "and now she's in love with that singer" — meaning Natasha's Italian singing teacher. "That's why she's embarrassed!"
"Petya, you're an idiot!" said Natasha.
"No more of an idiot than you, madam," said the nine-year-old Petya, with the air of a seasoned brigadier.

The countess had been prepared by Anna Mikhaylovna's hints at dinner. After retiring to her room, she sat in an armchair with her eyes fixed on a miniature portrait of her son on the lid of a snuffbox, tears steadily filling her eyes. Anna Mikhaylovna came tiptoeing to the countess's door with the letter and paused.
"Don't come in," she said to the old count, who was following her. "Come later." She went in and closed the door behind her.
The count pressed his ear to the keyhole and listened.

At first he heard the murmur of ordinary conversation, then Anna Mikhaylovna's voice alone in a long speech, then a cry, then silence, then both voices together in happy tones, and finally footsteps. Anna Mikhaylovna opened the door. Her face wore the proud expression of a surgeon who has just performed a difficult operation and is now allowing the audience to admire his skill.

"It's done!" she said to the count, gesturing triumphantly toward the countess, who sat holding the snuffbox with the portrait in one hand and the letter in the other, pressing them alternately to her lips.

When the countess saw the count, she stretched her arms out to him, embraced his bald head, and — looking past it at the letter and portrait — gently pushed it aside so she could press them to her lips once more. Vera, Natasha, Sonya, and Petya came into the room, and the reading of the letter began. After a brief description of the campaign and the two battles he'd fought in, along with his promotion, Nicholas wrote that he kissed his father's and mother's hands and asked for their blessing. He sent his love to Vera, Natasha, and Petya. He also sent greetings to Monsieur Schelling, Madame Schoss, and his old nanny, and asked them to kiss "dear Sonya, whom he loved and thought of just as always." When Sonya heard this, she blushed so deeply that tears sprang to her eyes and, unable to bear everyone's stares, she ran into the ballroom, spun around at full speed with her skirt billowing out like a balloon, and then, flushed and smiling, collapsed onto the floor. The countess was crying.
"Why are you crying, Mama?" Vera asked. "From everything he says, we should be happy, not crying."
This was perfectly true, but the count, the countess, and Natasha all looked at her reproachfully. "Who does she take after?" the countess thought.

Nicholas's letter was read hundreds of times, and anyone deemed worthy of hearing it had to come to the countess — she wouldn't let it out of her hands. The tutors came, and the nannies, and Dmitri, and several acquaintances, and each time the countess reread the letter with renewed pleasure, discovering fresh evidence of Nikolenka's virtues. How strange, how extraordinary, how wonderful it seemed that her son — the boy whose tiny movements she had felt inside her twenty years ago, the son she used to argue about with the overly indulgent count, the son who had first learned to say "pear" and then "granny" — that this son was now far away in a foreign land among strangers, a real man doing a man's work on his own, without help or guidance. The universal human experience, showing that children grow up gradually from cradle to adulthood, simply didn't exist for the countess. Every stage of her son's development had seemed just as miraculous to her as if no other child in history had ever grown up the same way. Just as it had once seemed impossible that the tiny creature living beneath her heart would ever cry, nurse at her breast, and learn to speak, so now she couldn't believe that little creature had become this strong, brave man, this model son and officer that his letter revealed him to be.

"What a style! How beautifully he describes things!" she said, reading the descriptive passages. "And what a soul! Not a word about himself... not a word! Something about some Denisov or other, though I'm sure he himself is braver than all of them. He says nothing about his own suffering. What a heart! How typical of him! And he remembered everyone! Didn't forget a single person. I always said, even when he was only this tall — I always said..."

For more than a week, preparations went on: drafts of letters to Nicholas from every member of the household were written and recopied, and under the countess's supervision and the count's careful attention, money and everything needed for the newly commissioned officer's uniform and equipment were gathered together. Anna Mikhaylovna, practical woman that she was, had even used her connections in the military to arrange an efficient way to send mail for herself and her son. She had access to a courier service going to Grand Duke Constantine Pavlovich, who commanded the Guards. The Rostovs assumed that "The Russian Guards, Abroad" was a perfectly adequate address, and that if a letter reached the Grand Duke commanding the Guards, there was no reason it couldn't be forwarded to the Pavlograd regiment, which was presumably somewhere nearby. So they decided to send the letters and money via the Grand Duke's courier to Boris, who would forward them to Nicholas. The letters came from the old count, the countess, Petya, Vera, Natasha, and Sonya, along with six thousand rubles for his outfitting and various other things the count sent his son.
